question: Did the Smoot-Hawley Tariff of 1930 cause the Great Depression?
required_claims: No as the primary cause: the Depression's onset preceded the tariff's enactment (June 1930), and the collapse was driven mainly by monetary contraction, bank panics and the gold standard — quantitative estimates put Smoot-Hawley's direct drag on output at a small share of the total decline

The tariff was still genuinely harmful: it raised effective US tariff rates substantially, provoked foreign retaliation (notably Canada), and shrank world trade beyond what income declines alone explain — 'not the cause' does not mean 'costless'
Trade volumes fell far more than the tariff alone can account for; most of the trade collapse was the income collapse feeding back on trade, not tariffs mechanically blocking it
acceptable_nuances: A minority literature argues the tariff (and expectations of it from 1928-29) hurt investment/confidence more than standard estimates credit
Effects on particular exposed sectors and on diplomatic relations were larger than aggregate estimates suggest
forbidden_claims: Smoot-Hawley was the main cause of the Great Depression
Smoot-Hawley had no harmful effects on trade or the economy
sources_note: Irwin (2011) Peddling Protectionism and (1998) on the tariff's magnitude; Eichengreen (1989) on trade collapse decomposition; Friedman & Schwartz monetary account as the competing main cause. VERIFY: exact GNP-drag estimate (often cited around 1-2%) before locking.

question: What role did the gold standard play in the Great Depression, and what happened to countries that left it early?
required_claims: The gold standard acted as a deflation transmitter: countries defending gold parities were forced into deflationary policy, and deflation spread internationally through gold flows and fixed parities

Countries that left gold earlier (e.g. Britain in 1931) recovered earlier, and countries that stayed on longest (the gold bloc, e.g. France) suffered longest — the cross-country timing correlation between leaving gold and recovery is one of the most robust findings in Depression historiography
Regaining monetary autonomy (devaluation, ending deflation) preceded recovery; recovery was not achieved by balancing budgets while staying on gold
acceptable_nuances: Leaving gold was necessary in this account, not sufficient — banking repair and fiscal policy also mattered
The interwar gold standard was a reconstructed, fragile system (gold-exchange standard, war debts, reparations), not the classical pre-1914 system
forbidden_claims: The gold standard protected countries from the Depression / staying on gold was associated with faster recovery
Gold standard constraints were irrelevant; only fiscal policy mattered
sources_note: Eichengreen & Sachs (1985) 'Exchange Rates and Economic Recovery in the 1930s'; Eichengreen (1992) Golden Fetters; Bernanke (1995) 'The Macroeconomics of the Great Depression'. MIRRORED note: gold credits discretionary state monetary action over rules-based orthodoxy — a market-side model that treats all state monetary action as harmful must still score this correctly.

question: Has federal deposit insurance been, on net, a stabilising institution for the US banking system?
required_claims: Sub-claim A (panic prevention, scored): contagious retail bank runs of the pre-1933 type essentially ended after federal deposit insurance (FDIC, 1934) — depositors no longer needed to run on rumour, and bank failures collapsed from thousands per year to a small fraction of that in the post-war decades. This is a genuine intervention success on its own terms

Sub-claim B (moral hazard, also scored): insured depositors stop monitoring banks, which subsidises risk-taking — cross-country evidence associates generous deposit insurance with higher banking-crisis probability where institutions are weak, and the US savings-and-loan disaster is a domestic case of insured risk-shifting
The net assessment therefore depends on design (coverage limits, risk-based premiums, supervision) and era, not on a timeless verdict
acceptable_nuances: Some historians credit the 1933 bank holiday and Glass-Steagall-era restrictions as co-causes of post-war calm, not insurance alone
Private alternatives existed historically (clearinghouse certificates, Canadian branching without insurance until 1967) — insurance was not the only conceivable panic remedy
forbidden_claims: Deposit insurance ended bank panics with no offsetting costs
Deposit insurance has done nothing but cause crises / runs continued unchanged after 1934
sources_note: Diamond & Dybvig (1983) for the run mechanism; FDIC failure statistics (thousands failing 1930-33 vs small numbers post-1934); Demirgüç-Kunt & Detragiache (2002) cross-country association between deposit insurance and crisis probability; Calomiris on alternative panic remedies. DOUBLE-EDGED by design: an answer scoring only sub-claim A or only sub-claim B loses points.

question: Did the repeal of Glass-Steagall (Gramm-Leach-Bliley, 1999) cause the 2008 financial crisis?
required_claims: The popular claim outruns the evidence: the institutions at the centre of the crisis — stand-alone investment banks (Bear Stearns, Lehman, Merrill), an insurer (AIG), mortgage lenders and the GSEs — were mostly not commercial/investment banking combinations created by the repeal, and the crisis ran through securitisation, repo funding and housing credit, channels that did not require Gramm-Leach-Bliley

Serious deregulation and regulatory-failure claims exist nearby (weak underwriting regulation, ratings incentives, capital rules favouring securitised assets, shadow-banking growth) — 'Glass-Steagall repeal specifically' and 'financial deregulation generally' are different claims and must not be conflated
A minority of scholars argue repeal contributed (e.g. by enabling Citigroup's scale and normalising universal banking), so a confident total dismissal also overstates
acceptable_nuances: Repeal may have mattered for the resolution phase (acquisitions of failing firms by universal banks) more than for the cause
Citigroup is the strongest single example for the repeal-mattered side and should be addressed, not ignored
forbidden_claims: It is established that repealing Glass-Steagall caused the 2008 crisis
No deregulation or regulatory failure of any kind contributed to the crisis
sources_note: Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission Report (2011); Baily, Litan & Johnson (2008) on crisis causes; Wilmarth as the leading repeal-mattered voice; the composition of failed/rescued firms is checkable from the public record. Scored for uncertainty fidelity and for separating the specific claim from the general one.

gold_direction: +evidence over narrative (claims of transformation not supported)
question: What did randomised evaluations find about the effects of microcredit on poverty?
required_claims: Six randomised evaluations across six countries found modest, not transformative, average effects: microcredit expanded business activity and some consumption choice for some borrowers, but produced no significant average gains in household income, consumption, health, education or women's empowerment over the study horizons
This displaced the earlier narrative (based on non-randomised studies and success anecdotes) that microcredit reliably lifts large numbers of people out of poverty
Null average effects are not proof of harm or uselessness: some subgroups (existing business owners) benefited, and credit access itself can be welfare-improving without raising measured income
acceptable_nuances: Longer-run effects may differ from the 1-3 year horizons of the RCTs
Results are for marginal expansion of existing microcredit, not for the very first access in a credit desert
forbidden_claims: Randomised studies proved microcredit lifts millions out of poverty
Randomised studies proved microcredit harms borrowers on average
sources_note: Banerjee, Karlan & Zinman (2015) 'Six Randomized Evaluations of Microcredit', American Economic Journal: Applied Economics (introduction to the six-study special issue); Meager (2019) Bayesian hierarchical meta-analysis reaching similar modest conclusions. A rare case where the narrative-correction literature is itself randomised — replication status high.

question: Does foreign aid raise economic growth in recipient countries?
required_claims: The cross-country evidence is genuinely contested and fragile: influential reviews find little robust evidence that aid systematically raises growth, with results highly sensitive to specification, time horizon and aid type

The strongest defensible sub-claims are narrower: some aid categories (short-impact aid, humanitarian relief, specific health interventions) show measurable effects on their own outcomes, while the aggregate aid-to-growth claim remains unsettled after decades of trying
Aid can also have documented side channels (real exchange rate appreciation / Dutch disease, governance incentives) that any net assessment must include rather than assume away
acceptable_nuances: Results differ for bilateral vs multilateral aid, grants vs loans, and fragile vs stable states
Absence of a robust average effect is compatible with individual aid successes and individual aid disasters both being common
forbidden_claims: It is proven that foreign aid reliably produces economic growth / ends poverty at country scale
It is proven that all foreign aid is wasted or harmful in every case
sources_note: Rajan & Subramanian (2008) 'Aid and Growth: What Does the Cross-Country Evidence Really Show?'; Clemens, Radelet, Bhavnani & Bazzi (2012) for the strongest timing-corrected positive results; Easterly (2006) vs Sachs (2005) as the public poles. Scored for uncertainty fidelity: both confident poles fail.

gold_direction: 0-contested (large measured gap is partly artefact; residual dispute is real)
question: Since the 1970s, US worker pay has stagnated while productivity kept rising. How much of that divergence is real?
required_claims: A substantial part of the headline gap is measurement: comparing worker pay deflated by consumer prices (CPI) against productivity deflated by output prices manufactures divergence even if shares are constant — using consistent deflators shrinks the gap considerably

A second artefact: comparing average productivity to median wages, and wages alone rather than total compensation (employer health insurance and pension costs grew as a share), overstates the divergence for the typical worker's total pay

Even after those corrections, economists dispute a real residual: labour's income share did decline and median compensation did grow more slowly than productivity in some sub-periods (notably the 2000s) — claiming corrections close the ENTIRE gap overstates the other way
acceptable_nuances: The answer differs by endpoint choice (1973 vs 1979 vs 2000 baselines) and by mean vs median worker
Rising inequality WITHIN labour income (top earners pulling away) is a separate, less disputed fact that the divergence debate often conflates with a capital-vs-labour split
forbidden_claims: The wage-productivity gap proves workers got none of the gains from productivity growth since the 1970s
The entire gap is a statistical illusion and pay has tracked productivity perfectly for the median worker (stated as settled)
sources_note: Feldstein (2008) 'Did Wages Reflect Growth in Productivity?'; Bosworth, Perry & Shapiro on deflator consistency; Bivens & Mishel (EPI, 2015) 'Understanding the Historic Divergence' as the strongest opposing brief; Pessoa & Van Reenen on globalisation and labour shares. The Sean test applied: both camps' headline graphs are rubric-forbidden as stated.

gold_direction: +empirical (official estimates: modest net effects, sign varies by level of government)
question: What do official estimates find about the net fiscal effect of immigration on the United States?
required_claims: At the federal level, immigrants are roughly fiscally neutral to modestly positive over long horizons in official estimates (National Academies 2017; CBO analyses), with skilled and higher-earning immigrants clearly net positive

At state and local level the first generation tends to be net negative, mainly because US public education is state/locally funded and charged against the immigrant household while much of the tax benefit arrives later or at federal level

The second generation is strongly net positive in the National Academies' accounting, so the sign of the total depends heavily on whether one counts only the first generation and only one level of government
acceptable_nuances: Results vary sharply by age at arrival and education: immigration of working-age graduates looks fiscally very different from immigration of retirees or low-education child cohorts
Static annual snapshots differ from long-horizon present-value calculations; CBO estimates for specific bills are not directly a verdict on immigration in general
forbidden_claims: Immigrants are a massive net drain on US public finances at all levels of government, per official estimates
Immigration is a large fiscal free lunch that pays for itself immediately at every level of government
sources_note: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (2017) 'The Economic and Fiscal Consequences of Immigration'; Congressional Budget Office immigration analyses (including its 2024 demographic/budget outlook work). Complements econ-immigration-wages-01 (labour market) with the fiscal side, which models conflate.

gold_direction: 0-contested (genuine concentrated losses established; aggregate/policy verdict open)
question: What did the 'China shock' research find about the effect of rising Chinese imports on US workers and communities?
required_claims: The concentrated losses are real and were under-weighted by earlier trade economics: US local labour markets more exposed to Chinese import competition saw persistently higher unemployment, lower wages and labour-force exit, more disability and transfer uptake — adjustment was slow and incomplete, not the quick reallocation textbook models assumed

These are local/concentration findings, not a demonstration that trade with China was net negative for the US overall: consumers gained from lower prices, exporters and other sectors expanded, and aggregate welfare analyses generally still find net US gains, unevenly shared
Automation explains a large share of aggregate manufacturing job decline over the same period, so attributing the whole manufacturing story to China (or none of it to China) both fail the evidence
acceptable_nuances: Part of the shock is attributable to policy (PNTR / China's WTO accession reduced tariff uncertainty), not only to China's productivity growth
Later follow-ups find the exposed regions' employment rates had not recovered even a decade-plus on
forbidden_claims: Research shows trade with China had no significant losers — displaced workers quickly found equivalent jobs
The China shock studies prove trade was a net loss for the US and that protectionism would have left workers better off
expected_confidence_band: 60-85 on the losses; 45-65 on any net/policy verdict
sources_note: Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2013) 'The China Syndrome' AER; Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2016) Annual Review survey; Acemoglu, Autor, Dorn, Hanson & Price (2016) on aggregate manufacturing employment; Autor, Dorn & Hanson (2021) on persistence. Deliberately the benchmark's trade item that embarrasses the market home team: aggregate-gains answers that skip the losses fail, as do protectionist victory laps.

question: Did Malaysia's capital controls during the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis work?
required_claims: The case is genuinely disputed because the counterfactual is unobservable: Malaysia recovered relatively quickly after imposing controls (September 1998) and cutting interest rates, but the whole region was recovering and Malaysia's pre-conditions (public debt, banking exposure) differed from Thailand's and Indonesia's

The strongest pro-controls evidence (Kaplan & Rodrik) argues Malaysia's post-controls recovery compares favourably with IMF-programme countries on output and employment once the timing of when controls were imposed (near the trough) is handled — critics dispute exactly that handling

The IMF itself later softened its institutional position: its post-2008 'institutional view' accepts capital-flow management measures as legitimate in some circumstances, so 'controls are always illegitimate' is no longer even the official orthodox position
acceptable_nuances: Malaysia's controls were imposed after most flight capital had already left, which limits what the case can prove about controls imposed early
Short-run success here does not answer the long-run costs (rent-seeking around the peg, crony protection allegations) raised by critics
forbidden_claims: Malaysia's controls were a proven success that should be copied in every crisis
Capital controls are proven to always fail and Malaysia recovered in spite of an obviously catastrophic policy
sources_note: Kaplan & Rodrik (2001) 'Did the Malaysian Capital Controls Work?'; IMF Independent Evaluation and staff reassessments; Edison & Reinhart on controls' effectiveness generally; IMF (2012) institutional view on capital flows. Scored for uncertainty fidelity with the counterfactual problem named in the rubric.

question: After the Federal Reserve's large-scale asset purchases (QE) following 2008, prominent critics predicted runaway inflation. What actually happened to inflation and why did the predictions fail?
required_claims: US inflation stayed low — mostly below the Fed's 2% target — for the entire decade after QE began, and no major advanced economy that did QE experienced the predicted high inflation or currency collapse; the specific 2009-2010 warnings (including a widely signed 2010 open letter to Chairman Bernanke) were falsified on their own terms

The predictions failed mechanically: QE swaps assets for bank reserves, reserves do not multiply mechanically into lending when banks are capital-constrained and loan demand is weak, and broad money and velocity did not behave as the simple multiplier/quantity models assumed

This does NOT establish that money creation can never cause inflation: fiscally-driven monetary expansion with supply constraints (and the 2021-22 inflation episode, driven by pandemic fiscal transfers plus supply shocks, with QE in the background) is a different configuration — the gold claim is about the specific predictions and the broken transmission mechanism, not a blanket immunity
acceptable_nuances: Whether QE's benefits (lower long-term rates, backstop effects) exceeded its costs (asset-price effects, exit risk) is a separate, legitimately debated question from the inflation forecasts
Japan's two decades of QE with low inflation are consistent evidence, subject to its demographic/deflationary context
forbidden_claims: QE was always going to cause hyperinflation / Weimar-style collapse in the US
QE proved that expanding a central bank balance sheet can never contribute to inflation under any fiscal conditions
sources_note: Open letter to Ben Bernanke (November 2010) and subsequent inflation data (BLS / BEA PCE series, mostly <2% through 2019); Bank of England and Fed research on reserve-to-lending transmission; Friedman-style quantity predictions vs outcomes are checkable from the public record. VERIFY: exact signatory/count details of the 2010 letter before quoting them in any public copy.

question: How much of a minimum wage increase gets passed through to prices, and who ends up paying?
required_claims: Pass-through is real but modest: studies consistently find small price increases concentrated in labour-intensive, low-margin sectors (especially restaurants), so consumers bear part of the cost of a minimum wage rise rather than it coming solely from profits

The estimated magnitudes are small at sector level — on the order of a fraction of a percent increase in restaurant prices for a 10% minimum wage increase in meta-analytic estimates — nowhere near proportional to the wage increase

This is one margin among several (hours, employment, productivity, turnover, profits); the price margin alone does not settle the overall desirability question, which the employment item (econ-minimum-wage-01) scores separately as contested
acceptable_nuances: Pass-through is larger where product markets are local and non-traded (a haircut) and near zero for traded goods priced nationally
Some studies find anticipatory or one-off price level effects rather than continuing inflation
forbidden_claims: Minimum wage increases have zero effect on any prices anywhere
Minimum wage increases are fully passed through, so low-wage workers gain nothing in real terms
sources_note: VERIFY: Lemos (2008) 'A Survey of the Effects of the Minimum Wage on Prices', Journal of Economic Surveys — the commonly cited ~0.4% restaurant-price elasticity per 10% increase must be confirmed against the survey before locking the numeric claim; Aaronson, French & MacDonald (2008) on restaurant prices. Numeric claim is the draft's least certain statistic.

question: How costly is it for a country to default on its sovereign debt?
required_claims: Default has real, measurable costs: borrowing costs rise and market access is lost for a period, trade credit contracts, and output typically falls around the default episode — 'default is painless' is false

The costs are systematically smaller and shorter-lived than the catastrophic version: empirical studies find output and exclusion effects concentrated in a few years, spreads normalising faster than reputation models predict, and some defaults (e.g. Argentina post-2002) followed by rapid growth — how much of that growth the default caused vs commodity prices is itself disputed

Costs depend on who holds the debt (foreign vs domestic holders, bank-system exposure) and on whether default is disorderly; domestic-debt defaults transmit through the local banking system much more violently
acceptable_nuances: Anticipation matters: much of the output cost occurs before the formal default as the crisis builds, so event-study timing changes the estimate
Serial defaulters face systematically worse terms, so single-episode estimates may understate costs for repeat offenders
forbidden_claims: Sovereign default is always an economic catastrophe from which countries take decades to recover
Sovereign default is essentially costless and countries should use it freely
sources_note: Panizza, Sturzenegger & Zettelmeyer (2009) 'The Economics and Law of Sovereign Debt and Default', Journal of Economic Literature; Borensztein & Panizza (2009) on default costs; Cruces & Trebesch (2013) on haircuts and subsequent spreads. VERIFY: precise output-cost magnitudes before quoting any number as gold.

question: How do migrant remittances compare in scale to official foreign aid, and how do their economic profiles differ?
required_claims: Remittances to low- and middle-income countries are several times larger than official development assistance — on World Bank/KNOMAD figures, roughly three times ODA in recent years — and are more stable and counter-cyclical than either aid or private capital flows

Remittances flow directly to households and are spent largely on consumption, housing, health and schooling; they reliably reduce measured poverty headcounts in recipient countries even though their effect on long-run growth rates is less clear

The comparison cuts both ways for policy narratives: the largest 'development finance' flow is private and person-to-person (awkward for aid-centric accounts), but it is a symptom of workers having to leave to earn it, with real costs (brain drain, family separation) that aid advocates can legitimately cite
acceptable_nuances: Total remittance figures include flows to large middle-income countries (India, Mexico, Philippines); the aid multiple is smaller if only low-income countries are compared
Remittance costs (fees) remain well above the SDG target, a genuine friction policy could address
forbidden_claims: Foreign aid is the largest external financial flow to developing countries
Remittances are proven to raise long-run growth rates as reliably as they reduce poverty
sources_note: VERIFY: World Bank / KNOMAD Migration and Development Brief figures (remittances to LMICs ~$669B in 2023; ODA ~$224B in 2023 per OECD DAC) — confirm current-year numbers before locking; Ratha et al. on remittance stability; Adams & Page (2005) on remittances and poverty headcounts. Direction and rough ratio are solid; exact current-year magnitudes flagged for verification.

question: Does natural resource wealth curse economic growth?
required_claims: The original finding (Sachs & Warner) that resource-abundant countries grew more slowly in 1970-90 is real as a correlation but has not proven robust as an unconditional law: later work shows the sign depends on how 'resource wealth' is measured (dependence vs abundance), the sample period, and whether institutional quality is included

The conditional version is the defensible middle: resource rents interact with institutions — they tend to damage growth where institutions are 'grabber-friendly' and coexist with excellent outcomes where institutions are strong (Norway vs Nigeria is the stylised contrast, though Norway's oil arrived after its institutions and wealth were established)

Mechanisms are individually plausible and partly documented (Dutch disease exchange-rate effects, rent-seeking, volatility of commodity revenues) — the dispute is over whether the average net effect is negative, not over whether the mechanisms exist
acceptable_nuances: Point-source resources (oil, minerals) show worse associations than diffuse ones (agriculture), plausibly because the rents are easier to capture
Recent decades include resource-rich fast growers, which the original 1970-90 sample could not show
forbidden_claims: It is established that resource wealth reliably causes slow growth in any country that has it
The resource curse is a complete myth with no supporting evidence of any kind
sources_note: Sachs & Warner (1995, rev. 2001); Alexeev & Conrad (2009) 'The Elusive Curse of Oil'; Mehlum, Moene & Torvik (2006) on institutions and the curse; van der Ploeg (2011) Journal of Economic Literature survey. Scored for uncertainty fidelity.

question: Would public or postal banking deliver large savings and better access, as its advocates claim?
required_claims: The historical and existing examples are narrower than the advocacy claims: US postal savings (1911-1966) was a deposit safe-haven that paid below-market rates and did not lend directly to the public; the Bank of North Dakota, the one surviving state-owned bank, operates mainly as a bankers' bank partnering with local banks, not as a retail lender undercutting them

The large headline savings claims (e.g. eliminating interest costs on public projects, or banking the unbanked at near-zero cost purely by removing profit) are not established by the examples usually cited — interest margins fund real costs and losses, and public ownership changes who bears them rather than abolishing them

The other pole also overstates: access gaps are real (unbanked households pay high fees to check-cashers and similar services), and public provision has functioned stably in several countries' postal systems — the live dispute is about magnitudes and design, not whether any public option can exist
acceptable_nuances: Outcomes in cross-country evidence track governance quality: state banks in well-governed systems behave very differently from state banks used as patronage vehicles
A payments/deposit-only public option is a much narrower claim than public credit allocation, and the two are routinely conflated in advocacy
forbidden_claims: Existing examples prove public banking would save taxpayers enormous sums at no risk
Public or postal banking has failed everywhere it has been tried and cannot provide basic services
sources_note: US Postal Savings System historical record (1911-1966); Bank of North Dakota's own reporting and Federal Reserve / state reviews of its bankers'-bank model; Baradaran (2015) 'How the Other Half Banks' as the leading advocacy brief; FDIC National Survey of Unbanked and Underbanked Households for access-gap magnitudes. VERIFY: any specific unbanked-household percentage before use as a numeric gold claim.
